@DrBruggeman Absolutely. How do we get Congress to reverse the ACA and get doctors out of hospitals and back into private practice?

Patients Are Telling Us What’s Wrong

Every day, I see patients who were evaluated at local hospital clinics one or two months before they see me. Many come to me because they feel they didn’t receive the depth of evaluation they needed.

I understand the enormous difficulty doctors face negotiating with insurers. But we need to get back to where we were: more independent, private-practice physicians with the autonomy to practice medicine the way it should be practiced.

And here’s the interesting part: if you build a good private practice, you will be busy.

Patients will find you.

Hospital systems are often overwhelmed, inefficient, and unable to meet the demand for timely, thorough care. That creates an opportunity for private practice.

We need more private-practice doctors—and we need to start using our collective leverage.

Do that, and you can regain your autonomy while providing the kind of personalized, in-depth care that patients are actively seeking.
@DrDimitrios Agreed.  Then go into independent private practice and do what is best for yourself and your patients.
@SteviKelly Agreed.  You can’t hide your head in the sand. I do find AI helpful especially when I see difficult patients.  I think It will be ancillary, not replacement.

As a neurologist, I’m not worried about AI replacing me.

Take Alzheimer’s disease. I have to talk to the patient, examine them, perform a mental status exam, look for Parkinsonism, order and interpret bloodwork, assess APO E genetic risk, and integrate biomarkers such as Ptau217/Aβ42 ratio, amyloid PET scan and EEG.
Then, are they a candidate for IV anti- amyloid therapy. 

Tremor? I need to determine whether it’s resting, action, postural, or evidence of Parkinsonism or maybe something else like due to meds —and then examine for the associated signs.

Weakness, numbness or burning? EMG/NCS requires interpreting motor and sensory responses and recognizing abnormalities in the waveforms and even the characteristic sounds of fibrillation potentials and denervation.

Those are just three examples.

Will AI assist neurologists- probably yes. Will they replace neurologists – doubtful! Lastly, I kind of think most patients are going to want to talk to a human being about all of this.
